The authors assembled 113 genomes from the RefSeq database, supplemented by seven newly isolated strains from an Australian thermophiles study. Phylogenomic metrics included Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI) and Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI), calculated for all genome pairs, alongside a maximum-likelihood tree built from 662 orthologous core genes identified with EDGAR 2.0. Orthologs were discovered by mapping CDS from the reference Geobacillus thermodenitrificans NG80-2 assembly against all target assemblies via BLAST, with Bacillus subtilis spizizenii TU-B-10T serving as the outgroup. The CDS were concatenated and aligned with MUSCLE, and a maximum-likelihood tree was inferred with FastTree. ANI and AAI similarity matrices were converted into UPGMA dendrograms using the DendroUPGMA web server. The combined evidence revealed that the genomes split into two main clades: clade I, containing all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and some Anoxybacillus species; and clade II, containing the majority of Anoxybacillus species. Clade I was further partitioned into three subclades, corresponding to Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and a third group proposed as a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. The candidate new genus was found to be most closely related to Parageobacillus based on ANI and AAI values. Two Anoxybacillus species, A. tepidamans and a genomospecies in clade I-c, were positioned consistently outside the three existing genera and were proposed for placement in Quasigeobacillus. However, A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus showed inconsistent positioning among the trees and could not be clearly resolved. The study emphasizes the importance of considering closely related genera together when constructing phylogenies or assigning genomic affinities, as narrower analyses can produce incongruent genus designations. The proposed taxonomic changes include the description of Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. with type species Geobacillus subterraneus strain KCTC 3922. The research highlights that whole-genome-based classification requires broader phylogenetic assessment to avoid misassignment of new strains. This work contributes to the ongoing refinement of bacterial taxonomy using genomic data, building on prior reassessments of the genus Geobacillus. The authors assembled 113 genomes from the RefSeq database, supplemented by seven newly isolated strains from an Australian thermophiles study, and applied standard phylogenomic metrics: Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI), Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI), and a maximum-likelihood (ML) tree built from 662 orthologous core genes. The combined evidence revealed that the genomes split into two main clades, with clade I containing all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and some Anoxybacillus species, while clade II contained the majority of Anoxybacillus species. Clade I was further partitioned into three subclades, leading the authors to propose elevating a third subclade to a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. Two Anoxybacillus species (A. tepidamans and one genomospecies) consistently occupied this third subclade and could not be clearly resolved into the three existing genera or the new genus, whereas A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus showed inconsistent positioning across trees and remained unresolved. The study underscores the importance of considering closely related genera together when assigning genomic affinities, as narrower analyses can produce incongruent genus designations. The proposed taxonomic changes include the formal description of Quasigeobacillus gen. nov., with type species Geobacillus subterraneus strain KCTC 3922, and reclassification of several Geobacillus strains into the new genus. The research highlights that broader phylogenetic assessment is essential for accurate taxonomy, and that the breadth of species assessed together requires further consideration. The authors note that the affinities of A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus remain unresolved, and that an alternative approach of merging these species with Parageobacillus would also necessitate merging Parageobacillus with Geobacillus, complicating the taxonomy. The study contributes to the ongoing refinement of bacterial taxonomy in the family Bacillaceae, and provides a framework for future genomic classification of thermophilic summary.title: Phylogenetic study of thermophilic genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and proposal of a new classification Quasigeobacillus
summary.authors: Carling (University of Canberra); Blom (Diversity Arrays Technology Pty Ltd); Georges (University of Canberra); Berenice Talamantes Becerra
summary.executive_summary: This study performs a phylogenomic re-evaluation of three closely related thermophilic genera—Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus—using publicly available whole-genome sequences. The authors assembled 113 genomes and applied multiple complementary metrics: Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI), Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI), and a maximum-likelihood (ML) tree built from 662 orthologous core genes. The combined evidence revealed that the genomes partition into two main clades, with clade I containing all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and some Anoxybacillus species, while clade II contains most Anoxybacillus species. Clade I further splits into three subclades, one of which the authors propose elevating to a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. Two Anoxybacillus species (A. tepidamans and one genomospecies) consistently occupy this third subclade but cannot be cleanly assigned to any existing genus. The study underscores the importance of analyzing closely related genera together rather than in isolation, as doing so exposes incongruences in current taxonomy. The authors note that when broader phylogenetic assessment is absent, genus designations for new strains can become inconsistent with the phylogeny of the complete genome set. The research demonstrates that combined phylogenomic analysis reveals delimitation problems that would be missed if each genus were considered alone. This work contributes to bacterial taxonomy by providing genomic evidence for taxonomic revision and highlighting methodological best practices for assigning genomic affinities. The findings have implications for how new isolates are classified and named in the future, emphasizing the need for comprehensive phylogenetic context. The paper also proposes formal taxonomic changes, including the description of the new genus Quasigeobacillus, reflecting the significance of integrating multiple lines of genomic evidence in modern bacterial systematics.

claims.description: Combined phylogenomic analysis of closely related genera reveals delimitation problems not visible when analyzed individually.
The genomes partition into two main clades, with clade I containing all Geobacillus and Parageobacillus plus some Anoxybacillus.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study performs a phylogenomic re-evaluation of three closely related thermophilic genera—Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus—using publicly available whole-genome sequences. The authors assembled 113 genomes and applied multiple complementary metrics: Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI), Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI), and a maximum-likelihood (ML) tree built from 662 orthologous core genes. The combined evidence revealed that the genomes partition into two main clades, with clade I containing all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and some Anoxybacillus species, while clade II contains most Anoxybacillus species. Clade I further splits into three subclades, one of which the authors propose elevating to a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. Two Anoxybacillus species (A. tepidamans and one genomospecies) consistently occupy this third subclade but cannot be cleanly assigned to any existing genus. The study underscores the importance of analyzing closely related genera together rather than in isolation, as doing so exposes incongruences in current taxonomy. The authors note that when broader phylogenetic assessment is absent, genus designations for new strains can become inconsistent with the phylogeny of the complete genome set. The research demonstrates that combined phylogenomic analysis reveals delimitation problems that would be missed if each genus were considered alone. This work contributes to bacterial taxonomy by providing genomic evidence for taxonomic revision and highlighting methodological best practices for assigning genomic affinities. The findings have implications for how new isolates are classified and named in the future, emphasizing the need for comprehensive phylogenetic context. The paper also proposes formal taxonomic changes, including the description of the new genus Quasigeobacillus, reflecting the significance of integrating multiple lines of genomic evidence in modern bacterial systematics.

Research Context
The introduction of next-generation sequencing enables discrimination among bacterial genomes to establish taxonomic thresholds. DNA-DNA hybridization was historically regarded as the gold standard for bacterial taxonomy. 16S rRNA gene sequencing suffers from low resolution when bacterial sequences are highly similar. ANI values provide higher resolution than 16S rRNA for detecting genome relatedness. AAI is recommended for distant genome comparisons because amino acid similarity is better conserved.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to perform phylogenetic and comparative genomic analysis of three thermophilic genera. The authors hypothesize that closely related genera should be studied together to resolve phylogeny. The authors predict that combined analysis will reveal problems in genus delimitation not seen individually. The authors predict that a third clade within clade I warrants elevation to a new genus.

Methodological Details
The study used 113 genome assemblies of the three genera from the RefSeq database. Thirty-two Anoxybacillus and seventy-three Geobacillus strains were downloaded from RefSeq. Parageobacillus was represented by seven validly described species with one assembly each. Seven newly isolated strains from an Australian thermophiles study were included. The included strains comprised 31 chromosome-level, 33 scaffold, and 49 contig-level assemblies. Anomalous assemblies with suppressed RefSeq status were excluded from the study. Methods were based on those used for reassessment of the genus Geobacillus by Aliyu et al.

Procedures And Architectures
The core genome was identified using EDGAR 2.0. Geobacillus thermodenitrificans NG80-2 assembly served as the starting reference for CDS identification. Orthologous genes were identified by iteratively comparing CDS against assemblies via BLAST. Bacillus subtilis spizizenii TU-B-10T was included as an outgroup in the core gene analysis. Five low-CDS assemblies were excluded and one duplicate was removed during core gene discovery. The obtained CDS were concatenated and aligned using MUSCLE. The maximum-likelihood tree was built using the FastTree software package. Two-way ANI was calculated using the ani.rb script with default parameters. Two-way AAI was calculated using the aai.rb script with default parameters. Draft genomes were concatenated with 100 N bases introduced between contigs. ANI and AAI similarity values were arranged into matrices and used in the DendroUPGMA web server. The UPGMA clustering method was selected to obtain the dendrograms. Genes unique to clade I-c were identified using BLASTn alignment with relaxed filtering criteria. CDS from Anoxybacillus tepidamans PS2 were used to identify genes present in all clade I-c members.

Key Results
The core gene set comprised 662 orthologous genes per genome used to produce the ML tree. The ML tree was produced with 114 genomes including the outgroup. The core gene ML tree splits into three major groups: outgroup, clade I, and clade II. Clade I consists of eighty-seven genomes. Clade II consists of twenty-four Anoxybacillus genomes. The ANI dendrogram was built with 114 genomes. The AAI dendrogram was built with 114 genomes. Anoxybacillus sp. EFIL, Geobacillus sp. MMMUD3, and Geobacillus sp. DSP4a have ANI of 97.99, 97.14 and 97.64 respectively. Anoxybacillus sp. CHMUD had the most distant ANI value with 95.03 and AAI of 95.81. A total of 6 CDS were found to be unique to clade I-c. The mean ANI and AAI values suggest the candidate new genus is more closely related to Parageobacillus. The GC content also suggests a closer affinity to Parageobacillus. The authors suggest placing A. tepidamans and one genomospecies into the new genus Quasigeobacillus. The positioning of A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus remains unresolved.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The combined phylogenomic analysis reveals delimitation problems not visible when genera are considered alone. Considering closely related species together is essential for constructing an accurate phylogeny. Genus designations for new strains can become incongruent with the phylogeny without broader assessment. Clade I-c is seen to be outside of the existing genera when analyzed together. The evidence supports elevating clade I-c to the new genus Quasigeobacillus. The incongruous positioning of two species leaves their affinities unresolved.

Contradictions And Limitations
Two Anoxybacillus species could not be clearly resolved into any genus. The alternative of merging clade I-c with Parageobacillus would require merging Parageobacillus with Geobacillus. The paper is a preprint not yet certified by peer review.

Claims
Combined phylogenomic analysis of closely related genera reveals delimitation problems not visible when analyzed individually. The combined analysis reveals problems in genus delimitation. Considering closely related species together is essential for phylogeny. The genus designation can become incongruent without broader assessment. Each genus considered alone would not reveal these problems. Merging clade I-c with Parageobacillus would require merging Parageobacillus with Geobacillus. Broader phylogenetic assessment is necessary before naming new isolates. Genus designations should align with the complete genome phylogeny. The evidence supports elevating clade I-c to a new genus.
The genomes partition into two main clades, with clade I containing all Geobacillus and Parageobacillus plus some Anoxybacillus. The genomes split into two main clades. Clade I contains all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and some Anoxybacillus. Clade II contains the majority of Anoxybacillus species. Two Anoxybacillus species could not be resolved into any clade. The two-clade structure supports taxonomic revision. The third subclade within clade I warrants new genus status.

Data And Code Availability
The assemblies are listed in Supplementary Table S1. Removed assemblies are listed in Supplementary Table S2. The Ruby scripts are publicly available in the enveomics package. The ANI and AAI similarity values are shown in Table 3. The unique CDS are shown in Table 4 and Table 5. The BLASTn alignment results are shown in Table 6. The best hit results are shown in Table 7. The ANI and AAI separating values are shown in Table 1. The GC content and affinity values are shown in Table 2.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Five low-CDS assemblies were excluded to preserve the core gene set. One duplicate Anoxybacillus Suryakundensis strain was removed. The relaxed BLASTn criteria were percentage identity 30%, bitscore 10 and percentage overlap of 1%. The candidate new genus is more closely related to Parageobacillus based on ANI and AAI. The GC content corroborates the closer affinity to Parageobacillus.

Ethical Considerations
The study used publicly available whole-genome sequences. The genomes were downloaded from the RefSeq database.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the core gene ML tree with outgroup, clade I, and clade II. Figure 2 shows the ANI UPGMA dendrogram with 114 genomes. Figure 3 shows the AAI UPGMA dendrogram with 114 genomes. Table 1 shows the ANI and AAI separating the candidate new genus from existing genera. Table 2 shows the GC content suggesting closer affinity to Parageobacillus.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is the proposal of the new genus Quasigeobacillus for clade I-c. The strongest evidence is the consistent positioning of two species in clade I-c across all methods. The future path is to consider closely related genera together when assigning genomic affinities.
